newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan must stay on reform path, caretakers say.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan must stay on reform path, caretakers say.

text.p: Pakistan's caretaker government is urging its successor to implement economic reforms and tight fiscal policies to meet an IMF-agreed deficit target.
With elections due on Monday, the caretakers installed by President Farooq Leghari after he sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5 have only days left in power.
"The economy is in considerably better shape now than when we took over," Shahid Javed Burki, Finance and Economic Affairs Adviser to the prime minister, told Reuters on Thursday.
"We pulled the economy out of a nose-dive. We are still cruising pretty close to the ground, but nevertheless the direction is right," he said in an interview.
"The single most important challenge for the new government is going to be to keep the fiscal situation in balance, to have a very close watch on both expenditure and collection of taxes."
Three months ago, just before Bhutto's removal on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, liquid forex reserves had fallen to $570 million, less than three weeks' import cover.
The rupee had just been devalued 7.83 percent against the dollar and a crisis package imposed to get the International Monetary Fund to resume a stalled $600 million standby loan.
Burki, on 90-day leave from his job as a World Bank vice-president, sought to rebuild reserves to $1 billion and won IMF agreement to resume and expand the standby arrangement.
He also launched an ambitious programme of economic reforms enforced by ordinances promulgated by Leghari. These will have to be turned into legislation by the new National Assembly.
Burki said he had met leaders of Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party, widely expected to form the next government, to persuade them to stay on the path he has charted.
The IMF insists that Pakistan slash its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) from 6.3 percent in 1995/96.

"I've already had discussions with some of the people who are likely to be important players when a new government comes into office and they understand how important it is to keep our IMF programme in place and make sure that those targets are met," Burki said. "It's going to be very difficult."
PML Secretary General Sartaj Aziz, who could well return to his former post as finance minister after the election, has in the past criticised IMF deficit-cutting targets as too harsh.

During his election campaign, Sharif has promised to resume work on costly motorway and airport projects, and to revive a "yellow taxi" scheme launched by his last government under which the jobless were given duty-free imported cars on easy terms.
Burki said he believed there was a consensus that his policies had been undertaken for the good of the country.

"We cannot afford to have crises every two to three years. Therefore it's important to have structural changes brought about. If we have succeeded in anything, it is to have succeeded at least in educating future decision-makers," he said.
Burki acknowledged that it had been an uphill task to rebuild reserves, which stood at $689 million on Thursday.
He said two IMF tranches worth about $80 million had come in later than anticipated and an expected quick-disbursing loan of $200-300 million from the World Bank had failed to materialise.
"They were not inclined to give us that kind of money shortly before a change of government," Burki said.

Pakistan had also been hard hit by a November 8 decision by Moody's Investors Service Inc to cut Pakistan's sovereign ceiling foreign-currency debt to B2 from B1. "It's been exceedingly difficult to borrow in the market," he added.
Burki said he was proud of the past three months' work to craft financial sector reforms, redivide federal resources among the provinces and renew relations with the IMF.

"My message to the international community is that Pakistan is poised to move forward in a very responsible way in restructuring its economy and producing the right kind of incentives for the private sector to come in," he said.
